Thursday, after closing.
Three weeks in, and Pema still apologises for everything. Today a customer's coffee order got mixed up at the bakery counter and the woman started raising her voice. Pema said sorry, remade it, and slipped a small butter biscuit on the saucer with a note: 'for the wait'. The woman left smiling.
Last week I told Pema 'good job!' after the lunch rush and got a shrug. 'You're just being nice, Ira.' Fair. It was vague.
So today, while we wiped the counters, I was specific. 'The mix-up. You stayed calm, you fixed it fast, and the note turned an angry customer into a regular. I saw her book a cake order on her way out.'
Pema stopped wiping. 'She did?' Then, quietly, 'I didn't know if the biscuit was allowed.'
'It was the best part.'
Later I saw her write something on a sticky note and put it in her apron pocket.

The loan camp at Kheda's panchayat hall ran from ten till four, and by the end sixty-two farmers had their crop-loan forms checked and signed. Not one had to come back.
On the bus back to the branch, Damini, the branch manager, turned round in her seat. 'Tanvir, that was the smoothest camp we've had in three years. Your checklist at the door saved hours.'
Tanvir smiled and looked out at the cotton fields. 'The sarpanch had told everyone what to bring, ma'am. And you did the planning. Honestly, it was an easy village.'
Damini frowned slightly but let it go.
That night, going over the register, he found he'd written one farmer's survey number with two digits reversed. His stomach dropped. He corrected it, then sat staring at the page. There, he thought. That's the real me. The camp was luck.

Anders put Hana's packaging design up on the big screen at the Monday meeting in the Copenhagen studio. The client, a small tea company, had approved it on the first round, which Anders said almost never happened.
'Hana did this,' he told the room. 'The fold-out label was her idea.'
People clapped. Hana felt her face go hot. 'It was a simple brief,' she said. 'And Mikkel fixed the typeface for me.'
Mikkel, across the table, looked confused. He had changed one letter spacing.
At lunch, Hana told herself that Anders probably praised everyone like that, that the client just liked green.

The front page closed at 11:20, and it was 11:02 when the night editor dropped a story on Nikita's desk. 'Needs a kicker. Quick.'
Nikita, three weeks at the newspaper, had heard 'kicker' a dozen times. She had nodded every time.
She searched her notes. Nothing. The clock over the news desk ticked. She thought of guessing, of writing anything and hoping.
Gautam, the chief sub-editor, was at the next desk, headphones on, fixing a headline. Her heart was banging.
She tapped his shoulder. 'Sorry, basic question. What exactly is a kicker?'
He slid one headphone off. 'The small line above the headline. Two or three words. Sets the tone. Like "Monsoon woes".' He put the headphone back.
That was it. No sigh. No look.
Nikita wrote the kicker in two minutes. At 11:18 she sent the page. Her hands had stopped shaking.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
For two years Elif and Vera had eaten lunch together at the kebab place near the office in Istanbul, every Wednesday. Since Elif became team lead in spring, she'd missed five in a row.
'Leads' lunch,' she texted the first time. After that, just 'busy'.
When Vera stopped by her desk to ask about the new release plan, Elif didn't look up. 'It's a leadership decision, Vera. You wouldn't really get the budget side.' Vera, who had worked on budgets longer than Elif, went quiet.
Some things Elif really couldn't share now: salaries, a colleague's performance review. That part was fair. But she also stopped telling Vera the small things, the jokes from meetings, the gossip about the new coffee machine.
On Friday, walking past the kebab place, she saw Vera there with two others from the old team, laughing. Elif felt a small sting, and then told herself she had outgrown that table anyway.

qa.q: How many Wednesday lunches in a row had Elif missed?
qa.a: She had missed five in a row.

qa.q: What was Elif feeling when she saw Vera laughing with the old team?
qa.a: She felt a small sting of loneliness or exclusion, then covered it by telling herself she had outgrown them.

qa.q: What could Elif do to keep healthy distance without looking down on old friends?
qa.a: She could keep private matters private but still join some Wednesday lunches and speak to Vera as an equal.

qa.q: How does Vera experience Elif's comment about not getting the budget side?
qa.a: Vera feels talked down to and hurt, since Vera has actually worked on budgets longer than Elif.

grounding: It shows a new lead skipping lunches with an old friend, talking down to that friend and sharing less, mixing natural distance with a sense of being above the old team.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
The staff room at Greenfields School still had the same cracked kettle, but Anand no longer drank tea there. Since he became head of the maths department in June, he took his lunch in the small HOD cabin with the door half shut.
Disha, who had shared a timetable and a table with him for four years, noticed first. At the department meeting on Tuesday she suggested moving the Class 9 test by a week.
'Let me explain it slowly,' Anand said, 'since you weren't in the planning meeting.' Two junior teachers glanced at each other.
He had also stopped forwarding the circulars. Disha found out about the new syllabus from the peon.
Some of it she understood. He had parent complaints to handle now, and things he couldn't discuss. But the way he said 'slowly' stayed with her the rest of the day.

qa.q: Where did Anand take his lunch after becoming head of the maths department?
qa.a: He took his lunch in the small HOD cabin with the door half shut.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling after Anand said 'Let me explain it slowly'?
qa.a: She felt hurt and belittled, since the remark stayed with her for the rest of the day.

qa.q: What could Anand change to keep a fair distance without seeming above his old colleagues?
qa.a: He could keep confidential matters private but still share circulars, speak to Disha as an equal, and sometimes eat in the staff room.

qa.q: How might the two junior teachers see Anand after the meeting?
qa.a: They may start to see him as someone who talks down to people, and feel less willing to speak up in front of him.

grounding: It shows a newly promoted head skipping the staff room, talking down to an old colleague and sharing less, beyond the natural distance of the role.
